title: AI promised less work. I've never worked more
titleZh: AI promised less work. I've never worked more
author: oorestisime
relevanceReason: 命中 3 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: The pitch was that AI would give us our time back. Write less boilerplate, delegate the boring parts, go home earlier. I am not complaining about the tools. I use agents for all of my engineering work now, and I wrote about how that setup evolved and why I still read the code. I can investigate and ship things that would not have been worth starting two years ago. But somewhere this year I noticed that I am working more than I ever have, and that it feels heavier than it used to. Not because any single task is harder. Because there are so many more of them, all at once. This post is me trying to understand that, with some data from my own GitHub history. The old load and the new load As a full-stack engineer, a normal week for me meant two or three serious tasks. A feature, a tricky bug, maybe a migration. Each one needed real focus, but I could hold one of them in my head at a time, finish it, and move to the next. Today my week looks completely different. I have several agents running in parallel: one implementing a change, one investigating a production question, one working through a review, another doing research I will need later. None of them needs me all the time. Every one of them needs me sometimes. That “sometimes” is the problem. Each agent eventually comes back with a question, a plan to approve, a diff to read or a result to make sense of. Responding means switching contexts: reloading a different problem, a different repository and a different set of decisions. Two or three serious tasks a week was tiring in a familiar way. Working with many agents is tiring in a new way. My attention is spread across more problems, and I find moving between them much more mentally draining. What my GitHub history shows I pulled my GitHub contribution calendar for every month from January 2019 to today and marked my roles at Bold.org, which I joined in January 2020: Full Stack Engineer until August 2022, Principal Engineer until August 2025, and Vice President of Technology since then. These are GitHub’s contribution counts, including private work, so they mix commits, pull requests, reviews and issues. It is a rough signal of activity, not a measure of value. 2019 is an incomplete baseline: my job before Bold.org used a self-hosted GitLab, so GitHub only shows what I did outside it. But the shape is hard to ignore.
The first part of the curve is what I expected:

My busiest coding years at Bold.org were the early ones. 2020 was my highest year, with 2,711 contributions. 2021 dropped to 1,839 and 2022 to 1,498. The Principal Engineer years were flat and lower. From August 2022 to July 2025 I averaged 114 contributions a month, against 173 as a Full Stack Engineer. My lowest year was 2023, with 1,189. The first months as VP of Technology looked the same. From August to December 2025 I averaged 111 a month, and December 2025 was my quietest month since joining Bold.org, with 50.

As a Principal Engineer, more of my work went into architecture, deep dives into concepts, setting up projects and planning, rather than fixing bugs or iterating on features. Becoming VP of Technology continued that shift, with even less feature work expected. At least until AI came along. Then 2026 happened:

I am back at my Full Stack Engineer pace. By October 27 I am at 2,102 contributions, already more than any full year from 2021 to 2025. Over the same period in 2020 I had 2,371, so 2026 is close to my busiest year but not above it. August 2026 is the busiest month in the whole timeline. 427 contributions, against a previous high of 319 in April 2020. My normal day moved back up. The median weekday was 3 or 4 contributions every year from 2022 to 2025. In 2026 it is 7, close to the 8 I had in 2020. Fewer weekdays without GitHub activity. Through October 27, I had 18 weekdays with zero contributions, compared with 40–46 across each full year from 2022 to 2025. These are days without recorded GitHub activity, not days off work. Heavy days became routine again. From 2022 to 2025 I had exactly one day per year with 24 or more contributions. In 2026 I already have 16, almost the 17 I had in all of 2020.

comments.author: ak39
comments.textRawHtml:
This resonates 100% with me. I am tired too.

This is what I think is the solution - I've tried it a few times with good results.

1. We need our own project or task plan. A simple forward-thinking TODO list is good enough. This needs to be prepared before the day begins. Daily.

2. Focus and limit scope. Focusing on doing ONLY what's on the list is the discipline I (we) lack and which we need badly.

3. Side quests are killing us. Allowing ourselves to veer off the planned daily tasks should require a complete away-from-the-keyboard planning session with pen and paper. Print it out but plan it away from the LLM. Use the LLM to summarise the problem, by all means, but do the thinking away from the LLM. The current TODO list needs to be the main input of such a deliberation. The output is the new TODO list. The objective of this away-from-keyboard exercise is simply to maintain control of the next steps.

On days where I worked with my TODO lists, I clocked out and joined the family for activities, slept sooner and better. On days I lost control of that list, the exhaustion mounted almost on the same day.

Make a finite list for the day, tick it off and go spend time with the missus, the kids or the dog. 2c.

children.author: matsemann
children.textRawHtml: Agreed. We're still bottlenecked when it comes to feature work because we need to think of the ideas, user test, talk with stakeholders etc. But somehow inventing loads of tasks to feel busy anyways. Those tasks are the side quests, things we normally wouldn't take on. It feels great to finally squash that bug or do that rewrite. But you're adding stuff onto everyone else's plate as well. Discussions, reviews etc, a constant barrage of new things to consider.

children.author: youniverse
children.textRawHtml:
I like this and then I also timeblock so I write out manually on paper every 30 minute increment, and then as the day goes you mark what you did in the previous 30 minute block. Doesn't need to be perfect but it kind of anchors you when at a desk and then it's interesting to look back at the end of the day and see how productive or unproductive you were.

Good strat.

children.author: vconnor
children.textRawHtml:
I work for myself, and I’d never use AI voluntarily. I mean, have you read the article in question?

I don’t see why I need to subject myself to burnout when I don’t have someone pushing me for higher productivity metrics. I enjoy thinking things through, planning, programming the bloody thing.

In all honestly, if I had to, I’d rather take drugs to be more productive than juggling a dozen agents. Being an overworked manager is no superpower.

comments.author: keiferski
comments.textRawHtml:
I think AI has also devalued a lot of work that previously might have been "mundane" but still felt like an accomplishment once you got it done. But now you can do that work to an ±80% quality level of the old, manual way, but in 1% of the time.

So the result is noticeably worse, but you basically must do it, because the efficiency gains are inescapable. This makes the work seem even more pointless, adding to the feeling that you're working more and accomplishing less.

children.author: core-utility
children.textRawHtml:
I see this directly. I'm an engineer but part of that is doing non-engineer work like making powerpoints, whitepapers, and generic work that's necessary but that I would delegate to someone else if I were high enough on the totem pole.

AI gives me the ability to do that stuff faster so I can focus more on the 20% and the quality of what I'm doing, not the nuance of formatting a document.

children.author: bagacrap
children.textRawHtml: AI makes up for a lot of crap tooling, but is often worse than good tooling. In this case "good tooling" would be a document template or formatting language that is easy/fast to use. What I have seen AI do so far if you try to one shot a PowerPoint deck is underwhelming to say the least. (To say more: it looks like a word cannon was used to splatter text on slides with random positions, colors, and fonts.)
